entries.title: Coefficient-Range Mitigation on an 8-Bit Coherent Ising Machine
entries.abstract: Mapping optimization problems to the restricted coefficient range of an 8-bit CIM can distort their encoded energy landscapes. We investigate whether three coefficient-range mitigation techniques previously studied for quantum annealing—interaction extension, bounded-coefficient encoding, and augmented Lagrangian penalties—improve end-to-end optimization outcomes. Experiments on weighted Max-Cut, multidimensional knapsack, and quadratic assignment show that the benefits are selective. At a fixed number of CIM calls, intermediate interaction extension yields higher mean best Max-Cut objectives, whereas aggressive extension degrades performance. Bounded-coefficient encoding improves the mean best feasible profit on one knapsack instance but not the other. Augmented Lagrangian perturbations increase feasibility when unshifted constraint penalties are too weak, but do not outperform the best unshifted penalty setting. Overall, coefficient-range mitigation is most effective when its strength is tuned to the problem and encoding, with aggressive mitigation potentially offsetting its benefits.

entries.title: From Entropy Source to Stochastic Bit-Stream: Low-Cost Converters for True-Random Stochastic Computing
entries.abstract: Stochastic computing (SC) encodes values as the probability of ones in random bit-streams, which allows arithmetic circuits with very low area and power and a natural tolerance to faults. The accuracy and security of an SC system depend on the quality of those bit-streams. Conventional generators build them from pseudo-random or quasi-random sequences, which are predictable, periodic, and correlated across streams drawn from the same generator. This work proposes three methods for converting the unbiased outputs of a true random number generator (TRNG) into stochastic bit-streams (SBS) with arbitrary target probabilities: a block extraction and comparison circuit, a counter-logic circuit, and a cascaded majority-logic pipeline. All three accept bits from any true- random source and are built from standard CMOS logic. They reach the accuracy of a software random generator for both independent and correlated stream generation, and they support the common SC arithmetic operations with error that falls with stream length at the same rate. Hardware synthesis results show that the converters offer favorable area, energy, and area-delay trade-offs relative to pseudo- and quasi-random baselines. Under injected soft errors, block extraction degrades no faster than the best deterministic baseline. By bridging raw entropy sources and application-ready bit-streams, this work makes true-random SC practical on standard CMOS.

entries.title: Collaborative Language Models for Semantic IoT Data Processing: Validation through Zero-Shot Human Activity Recognition
entries.abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) systems generate low-level sensor observations that are not directly suitable for process analysis and must first be transformed into semantically meaningful events. This paper investigates collaborative language models as a zero-shot semantic abstraction layer for converting such observations into higher-level event and activity labels. We propose a five-stage workflow comprising semantic mapping, semantic aggregation, temporal and contextual aggregation, specialized reasoning, and final event abstraction. The resulting labels and contextual information can subsequently be represented as event records for downstream Process Mining (PM) tasks. The approach is evaluated through Human Activity Recognition on the CASAS Aruba smart home dataset using eleven workflow configurations. The experiments show that collaboration alone does not guarantee improved performance: general-purpose auxiliary SLMs can degrade recognition, whereas assigning complementary specialist roles leads to better results and allows a smaller final classifier to retain much of the performance of a larger model. The selected workflow achieves a macro F1 of 0.643 in the 1.5-day comparison and 0.567 (weighted F1 0.680) in a one-week evaluation. Although trained ML approaches remain more accurate on this dataset, the results demonstrate a different design point: modular semantic event abstraction using off-the-shelf models without task-specific parameter fine-tuning. The findings indicate that the structure of LM collaboration and task decomposition is more important than simply increasing the number of participating models.

entries.title: Onnx2TEE: Automated Graph-Aware Model Partitioning for TEE-based Edge AI Protection
entries.abstract: AI models are increasingly being deployed at the edge. Since these models often require significant research and development to produce, are often deployed in potentially hostile environments, and downstream systems often rely on accurate data; protecting them from theft or manipulation is worthy of serious consideration. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), which provide hardware-enforced separation of software execution, can protect model weights but impose strict resource constraints, making full-model execution impractical for large neural networks. We present Onnx2TEE, an automated, model-independent pipeline that partitions ONNX models across rich, trusted execution environments for non-sequential feed-forward networks using graph-aware segmentation to preserve computational dependencies while minimizing boundary communication and reducing TEE-induced inference latency. Evaluation on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin using an Arm TrustZone TEE demonstrates that model parameters can be highly concentrated in individual segments, supporting selective protection of parameter-dense model components. The evaluation further shows that the generated trusted app's memory requirements depend on both computation and intermediate tensor sizes.

entries.title: AI, Bias, and Inclusion: A Two-Phase Mixed-Methods Study of Gender Bias, Awareness, and Trust in Artificial Intelligence
entries.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are widespread across fields such as healthcare, finance, employment, and criminal justice, with a substantial impact on the lives of individuals and society. However, it has been established that AI systems perpetuate existing social inequalities, particularly through biases that are not easily discernible. Such biases are embedded in the technical and social structures of artificial intelligence systems, making them difficult to detect. These biases challenge the concept of Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI), which recognizes diversity as the acknowledgment of individual differences, equity as fairness and equal access, and inclusion as the value placed on all participants. This study argues that fairness in artificial intelligence systems cannot be achieved by focusing solely on their technical aspects, necessitating a holistic approach. This study employs a two-phase mixed-methods design. Phase 1 applies computational content analysis to 360 occupational narratives generated by ChatGPT across four countries (Canada, Germany, India, and Bangladesh) using gender-neutral prompts to examine whether professions are predominantly associated with one gender and whether these patterns remain consistent across regions. Phase 2 examines the extent to which students recognize potential bias in AI, their trust in AI for consequential decision-making, and how these perceptions relate to themes in EDI and AI ethics scholarship. By combining output-level bias analysis with user perception data, this study identifies the empirical foundations necessary for future EDI-AI co-design frameworks, outlining the sociotechnical dimensions that such frameworks must address to be effective.

entries.title: MAQR: Lightweight Memory-Aware Q-Routing for Fresh Status Delivery in Multi-Hop IoBNTs
entries.abstract: This paper proposes memory-aware Q-routing (MAQR) for fresh status delivery over history-dependent molecular links in multi-hop Internet of Bio-Nano Things (IoBNT) networks. Repeated transmissions leave residual molecules, making link reliability history-dependent and fixed routing inefficient. Each link is calibrated from a spatial Markov model and approximated by three nonnegative decay modes. The resulting reduced memory state and packet bit composition provide an instantaneous link-success estimate. MAQR combines quantized memory and reliability descriptors with packet age, queue occupancy, and molecule reserve in a lightweight partially observable Q-routing heuristic. It is trained offline and requires only reduced-state updates and Q-table lookup during deployment. Across five independent training pairs and 20 shared evaluation seeds, MAQR reduces mean AoI by 46.9% relative to memory-blind Q-routing at 0.30 packets/slot while improving molecular efficiency. Frozen-policy sweeps further show comparable performance under weak memory and an increasing MAQR advantage as channel memory strengthens.

entries.title: Net-Gain-Optimized Constellation Shaping for the 5G NR DFT-s-OFDM Uplink: Probabilistic, Geometric, and Joint Designs
entries.abstract: Constellation shaping improves the achievable information rate of coded modulation. On the single-carrier uplink waveform of 5G New Radio, discrete Fourier transform (DFT)- spread orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM), the same shaping can also raise the peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR). A higher PAPR forces more power amplifier back- off and reduces the link budget. Prior work characterized this penalty for fixed probabilistically and geometrically shaped constellations, but did not turn the trade-off into a design objective. We optimize constellation shaping (CS) to maximize the net-gain, i.e., the sum of the communication gain and the PAPR gain, at the fixed spectral efficiency of 4 bits per channel use for 64-QAM. We apply it to probabilistic shaping (PS), geometric shaping (GS), and a joint scheme that combines both. As the coded block error rate cannot be evaluated inside a gradient loop, we use the achievable information rate as a surrogate for the communication performance and the PAPR surrogate as differentiable cost functions for the optimizer. The learned constellations are then validated on a complete DFT-s-OFDM link-level chain. Conventional Maxwell-Boltzmann PS yields a negative net-gain, but net-gain-aware optimization removes this deficit in every method. GS converts it into a substantial gain, as it not only improves the communication performance but also lowers the PAPR below the uniform 64-QAM reference, achieving the largest net-gain among the CS methods studied.

entries.title: HDMark: Holographic Multi-Bit Model Watermarking for Intellectual Property Protection in Hyperdimensional Computing
entries.abstract: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) models deployed on edge hardware are valuable intellectual property that is easy to steal, since a trained classifier consolidates its learned knowledge into a compact set of class prototype hypervectors; yet protecting their ownership through watermarking remains largely unexplored. We present HDMark, the first model watermarking framework native to HDC, which encodes ownership in the same hyperdimensional algebra the model computes with. HDMark maps a multi-bit owner identity to secret quasi-orthogonal carriers, superimposes them holographically onto the trained class prototypes, and verifies ownership with a statistical test. Across four datasets and three HDC learning rules, HDMark leaves accuracy essentially unchanged and verifies a 64-bit identity in 99.8% of trials at p < 0.001. We derive closed-form expressions for prediction fidelity and bit recovery that match measurements within 0.4 pp mean absolute error. The watermark survives fine-tuning and low-bit quantization, while attempting to erase it through noise injection, pruning, or overwriting severely degrades model accuracy. We further identify a dimension-permutation attack specific to HDC, which reorders hypervector coordinates to evade verification without altering predictions, and counter it through encoder realignment. Finally, an AMD ZCU104 FPGA implementation confirms that HDMark adds no hardware overhead, remains bit-exact under aggressive undervolting, and stays verifiable under timing faults until the classifier itself fails.

entries.title: A Self-Organizing Swarm Control Model for Underwater Robots Based on Turing-Type Reaction-Diffusion Principles
entries.abstract: In underwater environments, Global Positioning System (GPS) signals and high-speed radio communication are unavailable, and severe constraints exist on communication bandwidth and visibility; consequently, applying conventional swarm formation methods, such as the Boids model, which require the relative positions and velocity vectors of neighboring vehicles, is difficult. This study proposes a decentralized swarm control model that operates without a leader or absolute coordinates, relying solely on the number of received signals from two communication channels with different transmission ranges (inner and outer neighborhoods). The proposed model extends a cellular automaton model based on Turing pattern formation principles to continuous space and is grounded in the fundamental concept that swarms form as robots move toward regions of higher potential calculated from the difference in received signal counts. Specifically, stable behavior is determined through temporal averaging of potential values, hysteresis-based state evaluation, stepwise turning based on temporal differences, and vector composition with an external directional command. Two-dimensional simulation results demonstrated that autonomous swarm formation and control of swarm spatial dispersion via a morphological parameter are achievable, confirming robustness in maintaining swarms and high polarization even under communication dropouts where the communication success rate decreases to approximately 0.7.

entries.title: How Small Can a Single Shor Run Be? Limits and Constructions for secp256k1
entries.abstract: Most resource estimates for breaking secp256k1 with Shor's algorithm describe one long run per attempt, and the spacetime volume of that run, its peak number of logical qubits times its Toffoli count, sets its logical-error budget. Ekerå's tradeoff shrinks each run by using more runs, but how far it can shrink the largest run, and at what circuit cost, has not been determined. We minimize the volume of the largest run while every key is recovered with probability at least 0.99, within ten times the total volume of three runs of Häner et al. and 2⁴⁰ classical operations. We prove that a linear run fixed in advance, which starts its group register at a point and discards its label, reveals at most log₂(1+(|S|-1)/r) bits about a uniform key, where |S| counts its exponent values and r is the group order. With generic post-processing and the baseline's window costs, splitting alone then shrinks the largest run at most 1.86 times within the budget. To gain more, we make each exponent bit cheaper with windows that share one table point among exponent values related by six symmetries of the curve, on a point-addition core borrowed from the ECDSA.Fail leaderboard. One random scalar and one random start per run give every approximate addition uniform operands, and a bound on each run's outcomes certifies, for every key, a decoder that discards flagged runs. We count every Toffoli gate and every qubit of every run, and each configuration solved all 563 of its pre-registered simulated trials on secp256k1. The best one shrinks the largest run 3.87 times at 8.79 times the baseline's total volume, against 2.81 times for Ekerå's tradeoff on the same core, and its run is at least 2.6 times smaller than every design of Initio Intelligence.

entries.title: Triage Accuracy of Jev and Open-Weight System One Decision Models and Their Use for Early Emergency Recognition in Symptom-Assessment Applications
entries.abstract: Laypeople increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for triage advice, but LLMs answer in variable free text, which makes it hard to evaluate them for use in medical devices. Decision models, which assign a probability to each predefined triage category, may be easier to evaluate. To test their triage accuracy, we evaluated 16 decision models (14 open-weight, 2 proprietary) on 233 synthetic and 10,000 real-world cases, yielding 163,728 total assessments. The best models triaged 72.1% of synthetic cases correctly and agreed with an existing algorithm in 56.1% of real-world cases. They were more promising for recognising emergencies early: given only demographics, chief complaints, risk factors and red-flag answers, the best model reached an AUROC of 0.87. At a 5% error margin, it could decide for or against emergencies for about half of users. Decision models should therefore not replace triage engines but could shorten symptom assessments at setting-specific error margins.

entries.title: THeatA: Transport- and Heating-aware QEC simulation with Cooling Strategies for QCCD Trapped-Ion Systems
entries.abstract: The quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architecture is a promising approach to scalable trapped-ion quantum computing, enabling flexible qubit interactions by transporting ions between dedicated trap zones. Programs for such systems require operations beyond conventional circuit primitives: ion shuttling, physical SWAPs, trap splitting and merging, and cooling. Motional excitation accumulated during transport increases the mean phonon number of ions and degrades the fidelity of the two-qubit Molmer-Sorensen gates. However, existing quantum error correction (QEC) simulation frameworks do not jointly track per-ion motional excitation and explicitly schedule cooling operations with their transport time and heating costs. We develop a full-stack software framework for QEC experiments and simulations on linear QCCD systems with a single ion species, comprising an intermediate representation (IR) supporting QCCD-native operations, a compiler that translates syndrome-extraction circuits into the IR, and a heating-aware noise-injection pipeline that generates noisy Stim circuits. The compiler updates the mean phonon number of each ion throughout the schedule, and the pipeline derives gate-dependent error rates from the tracked phonon states and per-ion timing, enabling the evaluation of finite-size logical-error scaling of the rotated surface code under transport- and heating-aware noise. We show that transport-induced heating prevents logical error rates from decreasing with increasing code distance under the evaluated conditions, and that indirectly cooling the ion pairs involved in two-qubit gates, by merging them with precooled coolant ions immediately before each gate, restores this decrease. By sweeping the duration and post-cooling mean phonon number of an abstract cooling instruction, we characterize their trade-off and identify the region in which logical-error scaling is maintained.
entries.comment: 14 pages, 8 figures + 6 page appendix with 6 additional figures. Comments are welcome

entries.title: Pudding: A Retargetable Compiler for Processing-Using-DRAM Systems
entries.abstract: Processing-Using-DRAM (PUD) architectures exploit the physics of DRAM arrays to perform Boolean operations directly in memory, eliminating the data movement bottleneck in memory-intensive workloads. Several PUD architectures have been recently proposed which differ in their primitive operation sets, row allocation models, and execution metrics. These architectural differences are today hard-coded in emerging PUD-aware compilers, making crossarchitecture reuse impossible. We present a retargetable, end-to-end compilation framework for PUD architectures. The central idea is to make the architecture description a first-class object in the compilation pipeline: retargeting to a new PUD architecture only requires supplying its description. Built upon the MLIR framework, our compiler operates at two coupled levels. At the tensor level, it lowers high-level programs through bit-slicing, mixed-precision assignment, and integer-linear-programming (ILP) based placement to reduce the number of PUD commands and inter-bank data movement. At the logic level, it employs equality saturation to explore Boolean network implementations, with rewrite rules and cost functions derived directly from the architecture description. Evaluated on representative workloads across multiple PUD targets with the same compiler passes, our framework matches (and in several cases surpasses) architecture-specific hand-optimized compilers, while delivering retargetability and extensibility.

entries.title: World Models and the Law
entries.abstract: Current AI may have a model of how we use human language, but this does not translate into a reliable representation of physical reality. World models promise to fill this gap by learning how an environment changes over time and predicting the consequences of an action, and they are already used to steer robots and generate explorable worlds. This article asks how AI regulation in three major legal contexts, the European Union, California, and China, copes with the distinctive challenges they raise. I propose a definition and a taxonomy of world models based on who or what acts on their predictions, and identify the risks of misplaced reliance on them. I argue that existing rules tend to cover world models but leave three questions open, i.e., action provenance, trajectory validity, and the weight of simulated evidence, and recommend ways to fill these gaps.

entries.title: LIELLA: Private Edge Adaptation with Photonic Weight Streams
entries.abstract: Although photonic accelerators have shown promise for energy-efficient machine learning inference, privately personalizing large models across multiple edge clients remains difficult under tight memory, precision, and hardware constraints. We present LIELLA, a weight-streaming architecture that enables multiple edge clients to personalize a shared model through compact private adapters. The two proposed photonic adapter architectures accommodate both backpropagation and forward-only optimization while substantially reducing modeled client-side electrical energy consumption compared with electronic adapters. Under simulated hardware noise, clients sharing the same streamed backbone achieve nearly clean accuracy on QNLI and SST-2, even with attojoule-scale optical energy per MAC at each receiver. The architecture also enables hardware-aware adaptation among clients performing the same task, allowing their individual private adapters to achieve further accuracy improvements. For a gigabyte-scale TinyLlama backbone, LIELLA maintains a megabyte-scale inference memory footprint and kilobyte-scale persistent adapter storage per client, while achieving strong performance through forward-only adaptation. These findings further highlight hardware-driven opportunities to develop smaller yet more effective parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods and more accurate, noise-robust forward-only optimization algorithms.

entries.title: Who Gets to Do Computing Research? Rethinking Access, Funding, and the Cost of Research – How do we ensure that everyone with the ideas, ability, and desire to contribute to computing research can do so?
entries.abstract: The future of computing research will be shaped not just by the questions we ask, but also by who has the opportunity to pursue them. Major investments in advanced computing, including artificial/super intelligence (AI) and quantum computing (QC), are expanding opportunities for discovery and innovation. Pursuing these opportunities requires more than a promising idea: researchers also need time, infrastructure, technical expertise, and support to compete for and administer funding. Access to these resources varies across institutions and may shape who can participate and which research directions they can pursue. A healthy computing research ecosystem depends on research taking place at institutions with different missions and resources, not only at the best-resourced ones. Computing research spans a broad spectrum of resource requirements, from theoretical work and software developed by small teams to experiments requiring specialized hardware, large datasets, and substantial technical support. Preserving opportunities across this range requires understanding not only the resources needed to conduct research, but also the costs of securing them. What does it cost an institution – and an individual researcher – to participate in computing research? This article invites computing researchers, university leaders, funding agencies, and industry partners to examine how funding structures, access to infrastructure, administrative responsibilities, and institutional expectations affect research opportunities, and how meaningful pathways can be preserved across institutions with different missions and resources.
entries.comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, Computing Community Conference article initially posted on Medium https://medium.com/@computing-community-consortium/who-gets-to-do-computing-research-rethinking-access-funding-and-the-cost-of-research-43caacd7b71b

entries.title: MM-Open5x: Practical Conformal Electronics via Multi-Material Multi-Axis Additive Manufacturing
entries.abstract: Multi-axis, multi-material additive manufacturing enables the production of conformal electronic systems that are difficult to realise using planar processes and can offer enhanced performance; however, accessibility and reproducibility remain challenging. This paper presents MM-Open5x, an open and low-cost multi-material, multi-axis additive manufacturing workflow for practical conformal electronics. The workflow spans design, simulation, toolpath generation, fabrication, testing, and assembly, and is released alongside complete design files, toolpaths, and representative G-code. Representative case studies demonstrate both the benefits and limitations of multi-axis deposition in practice, explicitly documenting common failure modes, calibration sensitivities, assembly bottlenecks, and material variability. Rather than prescribing an optimal solution, MM-Open5x is presented as a transparent, reproducible foundation upon which a broader community can iterate, extend, and apply conformal electronics workflows across diverse application domains.
entries.comment: 4 pages, 5 figures, To appear in the Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Additively Manufactured Electronic Systems (AMES) 2026

entries.title: Analytical Modeling and Optimal GPU Provisioning for Disaggregated LLM Inference
entries.abstract: We present OSplit, an exact analytical method that enables efficient partitioning of a GPU L1 domain into prefill and decode workers, including sharding for classical and advanced GPUs. OSplit takes into consideration model parameters, enabling any inference model to be partitioned into prefill and decode workers with a goal of producing the maximum throughput possible. OSplit is based on a capacity model that takes as inputs the model, the loading scheme (batch size, max sequence length), and models an inference serving framework (vLLM) and computes the efficiency of each GPU. For this, we model H100 and GB300 GPUs, and model a scale-up domain, along with FlashAttention-based kernels. OSplit first computes an optimal collective generation policy, which gives inputs to the capacity model that enables optimal split of prefill and decode GPUs. We evaluate our scheme over H100 (NVL8) and GB300 (NVL72) using vLLM inference serving and show throughput, predicted and measured latency, showing near-perfect theoretical-to-measured values over leading LLMs (Llama and Qwen)

entries.title: BitShare: Sensitivity-Aware Binning and Bit Sharing for Compacting LLM Weight Storage
entries.abstract: Decoding with large language models at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, so the bits stored per weight largely set its cost. Group-wise integer quantization stores every weight of a group at the same precision, although the input channels of a group differ in sensitivity. We present BITSHARE, a codebook-free weight format that keeps the integer grid and the dequantizer of group-wise quantization but varies precision within each group. Sensitivity-aware binning places the channels of each group into three bins at fixed positions, and static bit sharing with optimal bit-value allocation lets the less sensitive weights share their lower bits, each stored once per group or once per pair of weights. A sharing-aware version of GPTQ chooses every stored value, with no fine-tuning and no codebook. BITSHARE has two modes. BITSHARE-U gives every group the same layout, so its decoder routes bits by fixed wiring, while BITSHARE-N chooses a layout per group within the same bit budget. With calibration on the Pile and at the same storage, both modes have lower perplexity than GPTQ at 3 and 2 bits on WikiText-2 and C4. At 2 bits across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, BITSHARE-N lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by up to 70% against SliM-LLM and up to 35% against GPTAQ. At the 2-bit perplexity of SliM-LLM, BITSHARE-U stores 13.6-19.4% fewer bits per weight, cutting DRAM weight traffic by the same fraction. A verified hardware decoder implementation synthesized in SkyWater 130 nm reconstructs BITSHARE weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.

entries.title: APUF-SNG: A Low-Cost Arbiter-PUF Stochastic Number Generator with Tunable Output Probability
entries.abstract: Stochastic computing (SC) encodes numerical values as probabilistic bit-streams and enables arithmetic operations using simple logic gates, offering a promising paradigm for low- cost, fault-tolerant, and highly parallel computation. However, the accuracy and efficiency of SC systems depend on the quality of the stochastic number generator (SNG). Conventional SNGs rely on pseudo-random or quasi-random generators, whose deterministic nature introduces periodicity, correlation, and bias, limiting achievable accuracy and robustness. This paper proposes a low- cost arbiter physical unclonable function (APUF)-based SNG that operates in near-metastable delay conditions to generate true- random stochastic bit-streams with controllable output probabilities. By selecting input challenges that drive the path delay difference toward a target value, the resulting output probability is governed by intrinsic device noise, eliminating the need for conventional random-number generators and comparator-based SNGs. The proposed design inherits the low hardware overhead and statistical independence properties of the APUF structure. A probabilistic model and a challenge selection method are developed to characterize and control the stochastic behavior. An 8-stage APUF-SNG matches the 1% mean absolute error of state- of-the-art true-random SNGs at 1024-bit streams and occupies 116μm^2 in 45nm, 2.5x and 7x smaller than the TRNG-based and Sobol-based generator designs, respectively.

entries.title: Coupled Dynamical System for Sparsemax Attention
entries.abstract: We present a family of coupled dynamical systems that compute sparsemax attention. Each system fuses query-key similarity and normalization into a single physical relaxation. Specifically, we cast sparsemax attention as a constrained energy minimization problem and derive a pair of coupled differential equations: one drives the energy minimization and the other enforces the constraint. At equilibrium, the system state gives exactly the sparsemax attention probabilities. We realize this formulation with continuous Ising spins and with Kuramoto oscillators. These relaxations run natively on emerging non-von Neumann platforms such as Ising machines, which have demonstrated orders-of-magnitude higher energy efficiency than digital processors, yet have so far been used mostly for unconstrained quadratic combinatorial optimization. Because analog hardware has limited precision and is noisy, we simulate both systems under these non-idealities, and inference quality degrades gracefully. Our formulation extends these emerging computing substrates from combinatorial optimization to attention, opening a path toward a new class of physical accelerators for transformer inference.

entries.title: Intelligence as a Founding Principle: The O-RAN Architecture for Artificial Intelligence and Its Reference Implementations
entries.abstract: Since its inception, O-RAN has established openness and intelligence as founding principles of the RAN, transforming closed base stations into disaggregated, multi-vendor systems with a hierarchical RIC. This article traces AI/ML in O-RAN through open specifications and reference implementations to 6G design. We examine how open fronthaul, RIC interfaces, cloud orchestration, and AAL profiles support control loops across multiple timescales, model management, and hardware acceleration. Commercial deployments and OTIC testing demonstrate multi-vendor interoperability. Open-source stacks and testbeds support pre-standardization studies of in-node dApps. Within this architecture, GPU-based AI-RAN platforms realize the inline High-PHY split on shared RAN and AI compute, providing one reference implementation path for the O-RAN AAL alongside other implementations on heterogeneous hardware. Vector instruction sets and analog in-memory computing offer longer-term options for improving energy efficiency. For 6G, extending intelligence to time-critical radio processing and mobile agent services calls for deadline-bounded third-party inference, energy-efficient RAN/Edge-AI silicon co-design, and agent session continuity across handovers. We propose a RAC that coordinates agents across tiers through local shells and a shared exposure gateway, with in-node operating bounds delivered asynchronously. We also propose Recursive Standardization, in which results from federated open labs inform candidate 6G requirements and standards review guides the next round of implementation and testing.
